newsitem.title: HONG KONG: British business confident on future in Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: British business confident on future in Hong Kong.

text.p: British business is confident of its prospects in Hong Kong beyond the colony's handover to Chinese sovereignty in six months, the new head of the British Chamber of Commerce in the territory said on Monday.

Patrick Paul told reporters he was confident that friendly relations between business and government would continue after the capitalist territory becomes a Special Administrative Region (SAR) of China at midnight on June 30, after more than 150 years of British colonial rule.

"I think the government after July 1st will appreciate a strong and supportive international business community, just as much as a strong international business community will appreciate a strong and supportive SAR government," he said.
Paul, a senior partner at accounting and consulting firm Price Waterhouse, noted that a survey showed that nearly 99 percent of British Chamber members expected to be in Hong Kong in the year 2000.
He said chamber members had a high regard for the SAR Chief Executive-designate, shipping tycoon Tung Chee-hwa.

Paul dismissed concerns of a possible backlash against British business once Hong Kong is no longer a colony, saying any impression that British business had enjoyed an unfair advantage in the territory was wrong.
Chamber members were concerned there may be a gradual increase in bureaucracy and corruption, and a decline in English-language ability after the handover, Paul said.
But he emphasised such issues were only possibilities and not necessarily tied to the 1997 handover or to Hong Kong, adding that the chamber would work hard to get its views across to the government.
"We will work more closely than ever with the international business community making sure that the voice of international business reason gets heard in government circles," Paul said.
"Frankly, we have a high degree of confidence in the likely government that will emerge after the 30th of June," he said.
Paul said issues such as freedom of speech only indirectly concerned business, but could become important.
Chamber executive director Christopher Hammerbeck said Britain was the top European investor in Hong Kong and China.

"At the end of the day, one of the insurance policies in the future for Hong Kong is a powerful and well-focused international business community," Hammerbeck said. "We are committed to the prosperity of Hong Kong."
